analysis.one_liner: Requires a background check and waiting period before any licensed dealer sells a handgun.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 23 cosponsors from both parties, the bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it unlawful for a licensed dealer to sell a handgun to anyone without a local permit backed by an FBI background check. Buyers would wait seven days once the FBI cleared them, or 30 days if the FBI did not respond, and pay a fee covering the permit's cost. Records from applications would be destroyed after 60 days, and states with stricter rules could keep their own rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence, since a background check and waiting period screen out purchasers who are fugitives, drug users, or otherwise barred from owning handguns under existing law, and give a cooling-off window for impulse purchases.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires a permit from a local law enforcement officer, based on an FBI check for the existing list of prohibited purchasers (felons, fugitives, unlawful drug users), before a dealer can hand over a handgun [S2][S3].
It imposes a seven-day waiting period after the FBI clears a buyer, and a 30-day wait if the FBI has not responded, giving police time to verify eligibility [S2][S3].
It requires that application records be destroyed after 60 days if no disqualifying information turns up, limiting the paper trail on lawful buyers [S2][S3].
It lets states with stricter background checks or longer waiting periods keep their own rules rather than overriding them [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun buyers face a waiting period, a permit fee covering administrative costs, and a 30-day default wait whenever the FBI misses its deadline. Licensed dealers must verify a valid permit and ID before every sale, and local law enforcement agencies and the FBI take on the paperwork of running the checks.

drawbacks.text: A seven- to thirty-day delay applies even to buyers with no criminal record, which can leave someone who wants a handgun for immediate self-defense without one in the meantime [S3].
If the FBI fails to respond within 30 days, the buyer must wait the full 30 days anyway, so slow federal paperwork can delay a lawful purchase [S2][S3].
Buyers pay a fee covering the administrative cost of producing the permit, and local agencies and the FBI absorb new screening work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is modest and targeted: it adds one permit-plus-background-check step to dealer handgun sales and sunsets the records on cleared buyers. The real cost falls on buyers who are delayed and on agencies that process the checks. The waiting-period-with-background-check idea later became national law in the Brady Act, but this bill itself was narrower and never advanced far enough for its design to be tested in a floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, forwarded to its Crime Subcommittee six days later, and sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Porter (R-IL) introduced the Armed Felon Prohibition Act of 1989 on April 3, 1989, with 12 original cosponsors [S1][S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on April 6, 1989 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime [S5].
The bill drew 23 cosponsors in total: 21 of 257 House Democrats and 2 of 175 House Republicans [S4].
No further action was recorded. The bill never left the subcommittee and received no floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun sellers and opponents of a federal waiting period were better off, since no permit or background-check requirement ever took effect. The public gained nothing, as the screening process was never created.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan: a Republican from Illinois led the bill and 21 of its 23 cosponsors were Democrats, so the record shows no party split; the bill died quietly in committee rather than through a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Licensed firearms dealers and the gun industry
industries.note: The bill would have required dealers to verify a local permit and ID before every handgun sale, and waiting periods plus permit fees would have slowed sales. Its interest in unimpeded sales ran against the public-safety screening the bill provided.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (local police and the FBI)
industries.note: The FBI would run the eligibility checks and local chiefs would issue permits, gaining new duties and workload funded by applicant fees. Their screening role serves the bill's public-safety purpose.
